title: Josiah and the Book Found in the Temple
summary: Josiah becomes king at eight and walks in the ways of David without turning aside. In his eighteenth year, during repairs to the temple, the high priest Hilkiah finds the Book of the Law, and when it is read to the king he tears his clothes in grief. He sends officials to the prophetess Huldah, who confirms that disaster will fall on Jerusalem for its idolatry, but promises that because Josiah humbled himself he will be gathered to his grave in peace before it comes.
story: Chapter 21 ended with the sealing of Jerusalem's fate under Manasseh and the murder of Amon. Into that darkness comes a child king who turns out to be the most wholehearted reformer in the history of Judah. The narrator's verdict in verse 2 is the highest possible: he walked in all the ways of David and did not turn aside to the right or to the left, words that echo the law's instructions for a king (Deuteronomy 17:20). The finding of the Book of the Law drives chapters 22 and 23, the great reform that forms the climax of Kings' story of Judah. Yet the chapter is honest from the start: Huldah's word makes clear that the reform will not cancel the judgment already decreed. What it will do is show what repentance looks like and give Judah one more generation of faithfulness.
historical:
Josiah reigned from about 640 to 609 BC, so his eighteenth year was about 622 BC. His reign fell in the years when Assyria was weakening; after Ashurbanipal's death around 631 BC the empire fell into internal conflict, and Babylon under Nabopolassar rose against it. That decline gave Judah room to act more independently, including in religion. Jeremiah began prophesying in Josiah's thirteenth year (Jeremiah 1:2), and Zephaniah also dates his ministry to Josiah's reign (Zephaniah 1:1).

Shaphan and his family appear repeatedly in Jeremiah. His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah from execution (Jeremiah 26:24), and Ahikam's son Gedaliah became governor after Jerusalem fell (25:22). Clay seal impressions from Jerusalem bearing names like those of this court have been found, including one of a Gemariah son of Shaphan, whom Jeremiah 36:10 also names. What the book Hilkiah found was has been discussed since ancient times. Many early Christian and Jewish interpreters, and most modern scholars, identify it with Deuteronomy or a core of it, because Josiah's reforms in chapter 23 follow Deuteronomy's commands so closely. Readers who hold to Mosaic authorship see it as an old copy of the law lost during Manasseh's reign; many critical scholars think it was composed or revised not long before and presented as ancient. The text itself says only that it was found.
cultural:
Temples in the ancient world were built with foundation deposits, and kings who restored temples sometimes reported finding older inscriptions during the work, so the discovery of a document during repairs would not have seemed strange. The collection of money at the doors (verse 4) follows the system Joash had set up generations earlier (12:9-15), and the note that the workers needed no audit because they were honest repeats the language of that earlier account.

Tearing one's clothes was the ordinary expression of grief or horror. To inquire of the LORD meant to seek a prophetic word about a situation, and it is notable that Josiah's officials go not to Jeremiah or Zephaniah but to Huldah, a woman prophet whose authority they plainly respect. She lived in the Second District, probably a newer part of Jerusalem on the western hill that grew in the late eighth and seventh centuries, perhaps with refugees from the north after Samaria fell. Her husband kept the wardrobe, likely the vestments of the temple or palace.
literary: The chapter moves from routine to crisis. It opens with the ordinary business of temple repair, told in the precise, bureaucratic language of payments and supervisors, and then Hilkiah's announcement breaks in. Shaphan's report to the king is comically understated: first the money, then, almost as an afterthought, a book. The reading of the book produces the chapter's turn, and the rest is inquiry and answer. Huldah's oracle has two parts, each introduced with "this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says": judgment on the place and people (verses 15-17), and mercy for the king (verses 18-20). The word "heard" ties the chapter together: the king heard the words of the book (verse 11), and the LORD says, I have heard you (verse 19).

outline.t: The Book of the Law found and read

doctrines.note: The written word of God, lost and neglected, is found and read, and it reshapes the life of the nation. God's word has authority over kings, and its recovery is the beginning of reform.
Josiah's response is the pattern of true repentance: he hears, grieves, humbles himself, and seeks the LORD. His tender heart is what the LORD notices and answers.
Huldah's word shows that repentance does not always remove the consequences of generations of sin. Judgment on Jerusalem still comes, but the humble king is spared from seeing it.

words.note: Torah, instruction or law. The word means teaching or direction, not only legal rules, and it came to name the five books of Moses. The Book of the Law found here is the written covenant instruction, and its rediscovery exposes how far Judah had drifted from the terms of its relationship with God.

Rakhakh, to be tender or soft. Huldah says Josiah's heart was tender, open and responsive rather than hardened. It is the opposite of the stiff neck that 17:14 says ruined Israel. What God valued in Josiah was not first his achievements but the softness of his heart before the word.

Neviah, prophetess. The Old Testament names several women prophets, including Miriam (Exodus 15:20) and Deborah (Judges 4:4). Huldah is consulted by the king's highest officials, including the high priest, and her word is received as the LORD's own. Her role is a clear example of a woman speaking with prophetic authority in Israel.

christ: Josiah's story shows the power and the limits of reform. A king rediscovers God's law, takes it to heart, and leads his people back, yet the law itself announces judgment they cannot escape. That tension points forward. Jeremiah, who began his ministry in Josiah's reign, promised a new covenant in which the LORD would write his law on his people's hearts (Jeremiah 31:31-34), so that what Josiah's tender heart did for one generation would be done within God's people permanently. The New Testament says Jesus established that new covenant (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8). Josiah is also a son of David who humbled himself before God's word, a small anticipation of the Son of David who fulfilled the law perfectly.

hard.q: Huldah promised Josiah would go to his grave in peace, but he was killed in battle. Was her prophecy wrong?
hard.a:
In 23:29-30 Josiah is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho, which seems hard to square with being gathered to his grave in peace. Several responses are offered. The most common is that verse 20 defines what it means: Josiah's eyes would not see the calamity coming on Jerusalem. He died before the Babylonian invasions and the destruction of the city, and was buried in Jerusalem while it still stood, which is peace in the sense promised. Some add that being gathered to one's fathers in peace refers to honorable burial rather than to the manner of death.

Other readers think the tension is real and was left in place by the narrator, since Kings was compiled after both events and could easily have smoothed it over. They suggest that the promise was conditional on Josiah's continued humility, and Chronicles (2 Chronicles 35:21-22) says he died after refusing to heed a warning that came from God through Necho. On any reading, the narrator did not hide the difficulty, and the promise that Josiah would not see Jerusalem's fall came true.

questions: The Book of the Law had been lost inside the temple itself. How is it possible for a religious community to keep its buildings and routines while losing the word of God?
Josiah's heart was tender when he heard God's word. What hardens a heart against Scripture, and what keeps it soft?
Josiah reformed Judah knowing that judgment would still come. Why is faithfulness worth pursuing even when it cannot change the larger outcome?
